title: Solutions, concentration and solubility
blurb: Name solute and solvent, calculate molarity, percent and dilutions, and predict how temperature, pressure and dissolved particles change a solution.
question: A 1 L bag of normal saline is labeled 0.9% NaCl. How many grams of salt does it hold, why does it conduct electricity, and why would warming it change the amount of dissolved gas but not the salt?

teach.body: Formally, a solution is a homogeneous mixture: one substance (the solute, usually the smaller amount) evenly dissolved in another (the solvent, usually the larger amount). In plain English: stir sugar into tea and the sugar is the solute, the water is the solvent. Water is the 'universal solvent', and water-based solutions are aqueous. Solutions can be gases (air), liquids (salt water, vinegar) or solids (alloys such as brass and steel).

teach.caption: Strong electrolytes dissociate fully; weak electrolytes only partly. Acids and bases are electrolytes too.

teach.body: Dilute and concentrated are relative words. To be exact, use molarity: M = moles of solute ÷ liters of SOLUTION. Health care often uses percent weight/volume: % (w/v) = grams of solute per 100 mL of solution. Diluting adds solvent but not solute, so the moles stay the same: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.

items: Molarity: 0.5 mol of solute in 250 mL. Convert: 250 mL = 0.25 L. M = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2 M.
Percent: 0.9% (w/v) NaCl = 0.9 g per 100 mL. In 1,000 mL: 0.9 × 10 = 9 g, so 9 g/L.
Dilution: make 100 mL of 1 M from a 5 M stock. V₁ = (1 × 100) ÷ 5 = 20 mL of stock.
Finish the dilution: 20 mL stock + 80 mL water = 100 mL of 1 M solution.

teach.caption: Solubility is the maximum amount that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. A supersaturated solution is made by carefully cooling a hot saturated one.

teach.h: What changes solubility, and what changes speed
head: Change
Solid solute
Gas solute
teach.caption: Warm soda goes flat and warm water holds less oxygen. Soda is sealed under pressure to keep CO₂ dissolved.
On the line: saturated. Below it: unsaturated. Above it: supersaturated. At 40 °C, 45 g dissolves; 30 g there would be unsaturated.

teach.body: Some properties depend only on the NUMBER of dissolved particles, not their identity. Adding solute raises the boiling point, lowers the freezing point (salt on icy roads, antifreeze), lowers vapor pressure and creates osmotic pressure. NaCl gives 2 particles per unit, CaCl₂ gives 3, sugar gives 1. In osmosis, water crosses a semipermeable membrane toward the higher solute concentration.

teach.h: Scenario: Gabriel and the saline bag
teach.body: Gabriel, an EMT applying to nursing school, reads a 1,000 mL bag of 0.9% NaCl. At 0.9 g per 100 mL, it holds 9 g of salt. Water is the solvent and NaCl the solute; the salt dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the solution is an electrolyte. Normal saline is isotonic with body cells, so it causes no net movement of water into or out of them.

teach.text: Stirring and heating change how FAST a solid dissolves; temperature (not stirring) changes how MUCH. Gases are LESS soluble in hot water. Pressure affects gases only. Salt LOWERS the freezing point. Molarity is per liter of SOLUTION, not solvent. And 0.9% w/v means 0.9 g per 100 mL, not per liter.

items: Solution = homogeneous mixture; solute dissolves in solvent (in salt water, water is the solvent).
Like dissolves like; ionic solutes give electrolytes, sugar and ethanol give nonelectrolytes.
Molarity = mol ÷ L of solution; % w/v = g per 100 mL; dilution C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.
Heat: solids usually more soluble, gases less. Pressure raises gas solubility only.
More dissolved particles: higher boiling point, lower freezing point, more osmotic pressure.

summary: You can now identify solute and solvent, predict what dissolves using 'like dissolves like' and calculate molarity, percent (w/v) and dilutions. You can also classify solutions as unsaturated, saturated or supersaturated, predict temperature and pressure effects and explain colligative properties.

A.q: In a glass of salt water, which substance is the solvent?
A.why: The solvent is the substance doing the dissolving, usually present in the larger amount: water.

whyNot.0: Salt is the solute: the substance that gets dissolved.
whyNot.1: Sodium ions come from the dissolved salt (solute).
whyNot.2: Chloride ions also come from the dissolved salt, not the solvent.

A.q: Why does an opened soda go flat faster when it is warm than when it is cold?
options: Gases are less soluble when warm
Gases are more soluble when warm
Warm soda holds more dissolved sugar
Warming raises the pressure on the gas
A.why: Gas solubility falls as temperature rises, so CO₂ escapes from warm soda faster.

whyNot.1: This reverses the rule: gases dissolve better in cold liquids.
whyNot.2: Sugar content does not explain the loss of fizz; gas solubility does.
whyNot.3: Once opened the pressure is atmospheric; higher pressure would actually keep more gas dissolved.

A.why: KCl is ionic and dissociates into K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that carry current: an electrolyte.

whyNot.0: Sugar dissolves as whole molecules, not ions: a nonelectrolyte.
whyNot.1: Ethanol also dissolves as molecules, so it is a nonelectrolyte.
whyNot.3: Distilled water has almost no ions, so it conducts very poorly.

B.q: 0.25 mol of glucose is dissolved to make 500 mL of solution. What is the molarity?

whyNot.0: 0.125 multiplies moles by liters; molarity divides moles by liters.
whyNot.2: 2.0 divides liters by moles; it is moles ÷ liters.
whyNot.3: 125 multiplies by 500 mL without converting to liters.

B.q: Stirring sugar into iced tea will:
options: let the tea hold more sugar
B.why: Stirring brings fresh solvent to the sugar, increasing the RATE of dissolving, not the maximum amount.

whyNot.0: The maximum amount (solubility) depends on temperature, not stirring.
whyNot.1: Supersaturation needs careful cooling of a hot saturated solution, not stirring.
whyNot.3: Solubility is fixed at a given temperature; stirring only speeds up dissolving.

B.q: A solution holds the maximum amount of solute possible at its temperature, and extra crystals sit undissolved at the bottom. The solution is:
B.why: Holding the maximum, with excess solute left undissolved, defines a saturated solution.

whyNot.1: An unsaturated solution could still dissolve more solute.
whyNot.2: A supersaturated solution holds MORE than the normal maximum and has no settled excess until it crystallizes.
whyNot.3: Dilute means relatively little solute; this solution holds as much as it can.

C.q: How much 5 M stock solution is needed to prepare 250 mL of a 2 M solution?
C.why: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂: 5 × V₁ = 2 × 250, so V₁ = 500 ÷ 5 = 100 mL (then add 150 mL water).

whyNot.1: 625 mL inverts the concentrations (5 × 250 ÷ 2); a stronger stock needs LESS volume.
whyNot.2: 50 mL divides 250 by 5 and ignores the target concentration of 2 M.
whyNot.3: 150 mL is the water added, not the volume of stock.

C.q: At the same molar concentration, which solute lowers the freezing point of water the most?
C.why: Freezing point depression depends on the number of particles. CaCl₂ gives 3 ions per unit, more than any other option.

whyNot.0: Glucose dissolves as 1 particle per molecule.
whyNot.1: NaCl gives 2 particles per unit, fewer than CaCl₂'s 3.
whyNot.2: Sucrose dissolves as 1 particle per molecule.

C.q: A compound's solubility is 30 g per 100 g water at 20 °C and 65 g at 60 °C. A student dissolves 50 g in 100 g water at 60 °C, then cools it slowly to 20 °C with no crystals forming. The solution is now:
C.why: At 20 °C the maximum is 30 g, but 50 g is still dissolved: more than the normal maximum, so it is supersaturated (and unstable).

whyNot.0: Saturated would mean exactly 30 g dissolved at 20 °C; it holds 50 g.
whyNot.2: It was unsaturated at 60 °C (50 g < 65 g), but at 20 °C it exceeds the 30 g limit.
whyNot.3: No crystals have formed, so the mixture is still uniform (homogeneous).

reteach.title: Sugar in coffee, fizz in soda
reteach.question: Hot coffee dissolves heaps of sugar, yet hot soda loses its fizz. How can heat help one dissolve and hurt the other?

blocks.body: Sugar (the solute) dissolving in coffee (the solvent) is a solid: heat helps the water pull sugar crystals apart, so hot coffee holds more than iced coffee. Soda's fizz is a gas: heat makes gas molecules move fast enough to escape, so warm soda holds less. Keep the cap on and the pressure keeps the gas in. Stirring just gets either job done sooner; it does not change the limit.

blocks.h: Heat and pressure, side by side

blocks.text: If the question says 'how much', think temperature (and pressure for gases). If it says 'how fast', think stirring, heating and particle size.

explain.body: Polar solvents such as water dissolve polar and ionic solutes. Nonpolar solvents dissolve nonpolar solutes. Oil (nonpolar) and water (polar) do not mix.

test.q: Why does cooking oil not dissolve in water?
options: Oil is much denser than water
Oil is nonpolar; water is polar
Oil molecules are held by ionic bonds
test.why: Like dissolves like: polar water does not dissolve nonpolar oil.

whyNot.0: Oil is less dense than water (it floats), and density does not decide whether something dissolves.
whyNot.3: Oils are nonpolar covalent molecules; ionic substances such as salt dissolve readily in water.

explain.body: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution. Percent (w/v) = grams per 100 mL. Dilution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂, because adding water does not change the moles of solute.

test.q: Normal saline is 0.9% (w/v) NaCl. How much NaCl is in 1 L of it?

whyNot.0: 0.9 g is the amount in 100 mL, not a liter.

explain.body: Most solids dissolve more as temperature rises; gases dissolve less. Pressure increases gas solubility only (Henry's law). Unsaturated < saturated (max) < supersaturated (unstable).

test.q: Which change increases the amount of a gas that can dissolve in water?
test.why: Henry's law: higher pressure of the gas above the liquid forces more gas to dissolve.

whyNot.1: Stirring changes the rate of dissolving, not the maximum amount.
whyNot.2: Lower pressure lets gas escape, as when a soda bottle is opened.

explain.body: Dissolved particles raise the boiling point, lower the freezing point and vapor pressure, and create osmotic pressure. More particles, bigger effect: CaCl₂ (3) > NaCl (2) > sugar (1).

test.q: Salt is spread on icy roads because dissolved salt:
options: lowers the freezing point of water
raises the freezing point of water
raises the melting point of ice
test.why: Dissolved ions lower water's freezing point (freezing point depression), so ice melts below 0 °C.

whyNot.1: Solutes lower the freezing point; raising it would make ice form more easily.
whyNot.2: A higher melting point would keep the ice frozen longer.
whyNot.3: Dissolving salt is a physical change; the effect depends on the number of particles, not a reaction.
